opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the transformer has been an incredible workhorse, but it has one fundamental limitation that becomes really painful in robotics and embodied AI: attention scales quadratically with context length. When you're dealing with language, you can sort of get away with it, a few hundred thousand tokens and you're fine. But a robot is living in the physical world continuously. It's streaming in video, proprioception, tactile signals, many times per second, for hours, days, potentially its whole lifetime. You simply can't keep everything in a KV cache and attend over all of it.

So what excites me about Mamba and other state-space models is that they compress history into a fixed-size state that gets updated recurrently. Inference cost per step is constant, no matter how long the robot has been running. That's much closer to how biological systems work. We don't replay every frame of our day to decide what to do next; we carry a compressed memory forward.

Test-time training takes that idea even further, and I find it really elegant. Instead of the hidden state being just a vector, the hidden state is itself a small model, and you literally run gradient descent on it as new data comes in. So the model is learning during deployment. For a robot, that's exactly what you want, adapting to a new kitchen, a new object, a slightly different gripper, without going back to the data center for retraining.

Now, I'll be honest, transformers are still the default for good reason. The ecosystem, the hardware optimization, the scaling recipes are all very mature, and these alternatives still have to prove they match transformers on recall-heavy tasks at scale. I think the likely answer is hybrids, some attention layers for precise retrieval and recurrent or test-time-training layers for long-horizon memory. But if we want agents that live in the world for a long time and keep getting better, I think we need architectures that treat memory and continual learning as first-class citizens, and that's why I'm watching this space very closely.

r001.rationale: The response says Mamba/state-space models have constant per-step inference cost, but does not identify greater inference efficiency as an advantage of test-time training models.

r002.rationale: It says the alternatives must prove they match transformers “at scale,” but does not call for scaling them to frontier-model size.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I'm not someone who thinks transformers are going away. They've earned their position. But I spend most of my time on robotics, on embodied agents, and when you look at the problem from that angle, the transformer's weaknesses show up very differently than they do in a chatbot.

The core issue is attention. Attention is quadratic in the length of the context, and it carries the entire history around with it. For a language model answering a question, that's fine, maybe even ideal, because you want the model to look back at every token. But a robot isn't answering a question. It's living in a stream. It's getting camera frames, joint states, tactile signals, at tens or hundreds of hertz, for hours. You can't keep appending that to a context window and re-attending over everything at every timestep. The compute per step grows, the memory grows, and at some point the thing just can't act in real time. Biology didn't solve it that way either. Your brain doesn't replay your entire life to decide where to put your foot.

So that's the appeal of Mamba and the state-space family. They have a fixed-size recurrent state, and inference is constant per step. You see a new frame, you update the state, you act. That's a much more natural fit for a control loop. The classic criticism of RNNs was that they were slow to train and couldn't remember long-range dependencies, and what the Mamba line did was show that you can get the parallel training efficiency of a transformer while keeping that recurrent inference form. The selectivity mechanism, where the model decides what to write into the state and what to forget, is really the key piece. That's what lets it filter a firehose of sensory data instead of being overwhelmed by it.

Test-time training is interesting to me for a slightly different reason. The way I think about it, the hidden state in a transformer or a Mamba is a fixed-shape tensor. Test-time training says, what if the hidden state is itself a small model, with weights, and the "update" at each step is a gradient step on those weights? So the model is literally learning while it's deployed. The memory isn't a cache of tokens, it's a compressed, learned representation that gets refined online.

For embodied agents that's the dream. A robot walks into your kitchen, and your kitchen is not in the training distribution. Your drawers stick in a particular way, your lighting is weird, your cat keeps walking through. You want the system to adapt in minutes, not to wait for the next pretraining run. Right now we fake that with in-context examples, and it works to a degree, but it's brittle and it's expensive. If adaptation is baked into the forward pass as actual weight updates, you get continual learning almost for free, and that feels like the right abstraction for a system that has to persist in the world.

I'd also say there's a hardware argument. Transformers are great on today's GPUs partly because we co-designed the two. But robots run on edge compute with tight power budgets. A model whose inference cost is flat regardless of how long it's been running is simply a better citizen on that kind of hardware.

Now, the honest caveats. On language benchmarks, pure state-space models still tend to lag at the top end, especially on tasks that need precise recall of something far back in the context, copying, retrieval, that kind of thing. Transformers are just really good at that. So my actual prediction is hybrids. Most of the serious architectures I see have a few attention layers for the things attention is good at, and a lot of state-space or recurrent layers for the long-horizon, streaming parts. That's not a compromise, that's probably the right design.

And the other caveat is that the ecosystem gap is enormous. Years of kernel optimization, tooling, scaling laws, intuitions, all of that is built around attention. A new architecture has to be better by a wide margin to overcome that inertia, not just a little better. So I'm not betting against transformers. I'm betting that for agents that live in continuous time and have to keep learning, the inductive bias of a recurrent, adaptive state is the one that matches the problem. And whenever the inductive bias matches the problem, that tends to win eventually.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts transformers’ growing per-step compute and memory with Mamba’s fixed-size recurrent state and constant per-step inference, and describes test-time adaptation as nearly free.

r002.rationale: The response does not call for scaling Mamba and test-time training models to frontier-model size to compare them with transformers.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility of treating context as something you learn from, rather than something you have to keep looking back at. In a transformer, you retain this growing cache of past tokens, and attention lets you retrieve information from it. That’s powerful, but as the context gets longer, storing and accessing that history becomes expensive.

Mamba takes a different approach: it updates a compact state as new information comes in. Test-time training takes that idea in another direction: what if the model updates a small internal learner as it processes the sequence? Your history is then represented partly by what that learner has learned.

For an agent processing a continuous stream of video or interacting with the world, that’s a very interesting possibility. You want it to accumulate experience without carrying around every observation forever.

The tradeoff is that compression can lose information. Attention is very good at reaching back and finding a specific detail. So I wouldn’t say these approaches automatically replace transformers. The exciting question is whether we can combine efficient, adaptive memory with that ability to retrieve precisely when we need to.

r001.rationale: It contrasts transformers’ growing, costly context cache with Mamba’s compact state and test-time training’s small internal learner, conveying greater inference efficiency.

r002.rationale: It does not call for scaling these models to frontier-model size or comparing them at that scale.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the idea that a model’s memory doesn’t have to be a growing list of tokens. With a transformer, as you give it more context, you keep more information around and pay to attend to it. That’s very powerful, but it gets expensive when you’re thinking about an agent processing a continuous stream of video or interacting with the world for hours.

Mamba takes a different approach: it updates a fixed-size state as new information comes in. So the question becomes, can you learn what to retain and what to forget? You get very efficient streaming, although compressing history into a state creates its own challenges, especially when you need to retrieve an exact detail.

Test-time training pushes that idea further. Instead of just updating an activation, you update a small model as you process the sequence. Learning itself becomes the mechanism for storing information. I find that compelling because an agent should be able to adapt from its experience while it’s running.

I wouldn’t say either approach has settled the question of what replaces transformers. But they open up a much richer design space: explicit context, compressed state, and memory stored through learning. The most interesting systems may combine all three.

r001.rationale: The response says Mamba enables efficient streaming and notes transformer costs for long contexts, but it does not clearly claim greater inference efficiency for test-time training models.

r002.rationale: The response does not call for scaling either approach to frontier-model size to compare them with transformers.
